html:
Tlinoit is the map's spelling for the Tlingit, the Indigenous people of the southeast Alaska coast and islands. The area drawn for 1500 also stretches west along the Gulf of Alaska, the land of the Eyak and Ahtna and others.

The Tlingit lived from salmon, halibut and sea mammals, and built cedar plank houses and great canoes. Their society was split into two halves, Raven and Eagle or Wolf, and into clans that owned land, crests and stories shown on totem poles. They traded with inland peoples over the mountain passes and with the Haida to the south.

In 1799 the Russian-American Company built a fort at Sitka. The Tlingit destroyed it in 1802; the Russians took the site back by force in 1804, and Sitka became the capital of Russian America until the Alaska Purchase in 1867. See Lingít Aaní.
